title: Function types, lambdas & the inline family
scopeHtml: Scope: function types and higher-order functions, how lambdas compile (classes vs invokedynamic), closure capture, inline / noinline / crossinline, non-local returns and labels, reified type parameters, and when not to inline. SAM, references, receivers and defaults live in chunk 06.

questions.promptHtml: What is a higher-order function in Kotlin, and how do function types like (Int) -> String or (() -> Unit)? work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the foundation for everything else in this area (inline, lambdas, Flow operators, Compose). They check whether you treat functions as values with real types, including nullability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A higher-order function takes a function as a parameter or returns one. Kotlin has real function types: (Int) -> String means "takes an Int, returns a String". You can store them in variables, pass them around and call them with f(x) or f.invoke(x). A function type can be nullable, written (() -> Unit)?, and then you call it with f?.invoke(). Parameter names inside the type, like (userId: String) -> Unit, are documentation only.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A function type has three parts: an optional receiver, a parameter list and a return type.

Type Meaning
() -> Unit no params, returns nothing useful
(Int, Int) -> Int two Ints in, Int out
((String) -> Unit)? nullable function value (note the extra parentheses)
String.(Int) -> Char function with receiver (chunk 06 covers receivers)
suspend () -> Unit suspend function type (coroutines chunks)
() -> () -> Unit returns a function; arrows group to the right

Ways to get a value of a function type:

  1. A lambda literal: { x: Int -> x * 2 }
  2. An anonymous function: fun(x: Int): Int = x * 2
  3. A function reference: ::double (chunk 06)
  4. An instance of a class that implements the function type: class Doubler : (Int) -> Int { override fun invoke(x: Int) = x * 2 }

Calling: f(3) is sugar for f.invoke(3). For a nullable type, f(3) does not compile. You need f?.invoke(3).

Returning functions is how you build factories and curried helpers:

fun adder(n: Int): (Int) -> Int = { it + n }
val add5 = adder(5)   // add5 captures n = 5
add5(10)              // 15

The standard library is built on this idea: map, filter, let, use, repeat, synchronized, Flow.map, Compose onClick: () -> Unit are all higher-order functions.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Higher-order: takes a function
fun <T> retryTimes(times: Int, block: () -> T): T {
    var last: Throwable? = null
    repeat(times) {
        try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e }
    }
    throw last ?: IllegalStateException("times must be > 0")
}

class Button {
    // Nullable function type: "no listener" is a valid state
    var onClick: (() -> Unit)? = null
    fun performClick() {
        onClick?.invoke()     // correct
        // onClick()          // does not compile: reference has a nullable type
    }
}

// Typealias keeps signatures readable
typealias OnItemClick = (position: Int, id: Long) -> Unit

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing (() -> Unit)? as () -> Unit?. The second is a function that returns Unit?, not a nullable function.
  • Assuming parameter names in a function type are enforced at call sites. They are not; you cannot call f(position = 1) on a function-type value.
  • Exposing very long function types in public APIs instead of a typealias or fun interface. Readability drops fast with nested types.
  • Forgetting that each function-typed property you store keeps everything it captures alive (see Q080).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the difference between (A, B) -> C and A.(B) -> C? → Same JVM shape (Function2<A, B, C>), and values are assignable between them. The receiver form only changes how the lambda body sees the first argument (this). Chunk 06 goes deeper.
  2. Can a class implement a function type? → Yes, class X : (Int) -> Int. It must override invoke. Rarely needed; a fun interface is usually clearer.
  3. When would you pick a fun interface over a function type in an API? → When you want a named concept, Java callers, KDoc on the type, or room to add default methods later. Function types are lighter for local or internal callbacks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "a function that takes a lambda". The senior answer covers nullable function types and ?.invoke(), notes that function-typed parameters are what make inline worthwhile, and treats a stored callback as a lifetime decision because it holds a reference to everything it captured.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A callback stored as var onClick: (() -> Unit)? on a long-lived object (an adapter kept in a ViewModel or a singleton) is a common way Activities leak. The type is fine; who holds it and for how long is the bug.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through Kotlin lambda syntax: trailing lambdas, it, what the lambda returns, and what return means inside one.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many real bugs come from not knowing what a lambda returns or where a return goes. This question filters people who write lambdas by copying patterns.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A lambda is { params -> body }. If it has exactly one parameter, I can skip the name and use it. If the last parameter of a function is a function, I can move the lambda outside the parentheses, and drop the parentheses if it is the only argument. The value of the last expression is what the lambda returns; there is no return needed. A bare return inside a lambda is only allowed if the lambda is passed to an inline function, and then it returns from the enclosing function, not the lambda. To return from just the lambda I use a label, return@map.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Syntax rules, in the order people trip over them:

Rule Example
Full form val f: (Int, Int) -> Int = { a: Int, b: Int -> a + b }
Types inferred from expected type val f: (Int, Int) -> Int = { a, b -> a + b }
Single param becomes it list.filter { it > 0 }
Unused param as _ map.forEach { (_, value) -> println(value) }
Destructuring param map.map { (k, v) -> "$k=$v" }
Trailing lambda repeat(3) { println(it) }
Only argument, no parens run { compute() }
Last expression is the result { x: Int -> val y = x * 2; y + 1 } returns y + 1

What does the lambda return?

  • The type of the last expression, checked against the expected return type.
  • If the expected type is () -> Unit, the last expression's value is ignored, so { list.add(x) } is fine even though add returns Boolean.
  • An if without else as the last expression has type Unit, which surprises people in map { if (it > 0) it } (the result type becomes List<Any> or a compile error depending on context).

What does return do?

fun outer() {
    list.forEach {          // forEach is inline
        if (it == 0) return // returns from outer()  -- non-local return
    }
    run {                   // run is inline
        return              // returns from outer()
    }
    val f = { return }      // ERROR: 'return' is not allowed here (f is not inlined)
    list.map { if (it == 0) return@map -1; it }  // returns -1 from this lambda only
}

Q082 goes into non-local returns and labels in depth.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class User(val id: String, val age: Int)

fun adultsIds(users: List<User>): List<String> =
    users
        .filter { it.age >= 18 }           // `it` is the single param
        .map { user -> user.id }           // named param for readability
        .sortedBy { it }                   // last expression is the key

// Trap: last expression decides the type
val labels = listOf(1, -1, 2).map { n ->
    if (n > 0) "positive" else "non-positive"   // String; without else this breaks
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Nesting it inside another lambda that also has it. The inner it shadows the outer one; name at least the outer parameter.
  • Writing return x at the end of a lambda out of Java habit. In a non-inline lambda it does not compile; in an inline one it returns from the outer function, which is usually a bug.
  • Thinking { } passed where () -> Unit is expected returns something. It returns Unit.
  • Putting a lambda with side effects as the last expression of a Unit lambda and expecting the return value to be used.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can I pass { list.add(x) } where () -> Unit is expected? → For an expected Unit return type, the compiler coerces the last expression to Unit.
  2. How do I return early from a lambda without leaving the outer function? → return@label (implicit label is the function name, like return@forEach) or use an anonymous function fun(x) { return }.
  3. Why does Kotlin forbid bare return in a non-inline lambda? → The lambda may run after the outer function has already returned, on another thread, or never. There is no frame to return from. Inline lambdas are pasted into the caller, so the frame exists.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists syntax. The senior answer explains that "last expression is the value" plus "bare return goes to the enclosing function only for inline lambdas" is a consistent design, and points out the readability rule: name parameters once nesting starts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A return inside forEach that was meant to "skip this item" ends the whole function. It ships because the happy path still works; see Q087 for a real version of this bug.

questions.promptHtml: What does a Kotlin function type like (Int) -> Int become in JVM bytecode, and what does that cost at runtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can reason below the syntax: interfaces, generics, boxing. That reasoning is what justifies inline.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On the JVM, (Int) -> Int is the interface kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Integer, Integer> with a single invoke method. Because it is generic and JVM generics are erased, the parameters and result are passed as objects, so primitives get boxed when you call through the interface. There are Function0 to Function22; bigger arities use FunctionN with a vararg invoke (since Kotlin 1.3). So each call through a function type is an interface call, often with boxing, plus whatever allocation created the lambda object.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kotlin type                 JVM type
() -> Unit                  Function0<Unit>
(Int) -> Int                Function1<Integer, Integer>   invoke(Object): Object
(String, Int) -> Boolean    Function2<String, Integer, Boolean>
String.(Int) -> Unit        Function2<String, Integer, Unit>   (receiver = first param)
23+ parameters              FunctionN<R>   invoke(vararg Object)
suspend (Int) -> Int        Function2<Integer, Continuation<Integer>, Object>  (CPS, chunk 13)

Costs, from most to least important in practice:

  1. Allocation of the function object. A lambda that captures variables is a new object each time the lambda expression is evaluated. A non-capturing lambda is usually a cached singleton (Q079).
  2. Boxing. (Int) -> Int invoked through the interface boxes the argument and the result. Integer.valueOf caches -128..127, so small values do not allocate, but large ones do. In a loop over 1M elements, that is up to 2M Integer objects.
  3. Interface dispatch. invoke is an interface call. The JIT on ART can often devirtualize monomorphic call sites, but megamorphic sites (one generic helper called with many different lambdas) stay slower.
  4. Unit return. A () -> Unit lambda returns the Unit singleton; no allocation, just a reference.

The compiled lambda class (pre-2.0 scheme) also has a "bridge" invoke(Object): Object that casts and unboxes before calling the specialized invoke(I)I. So the body itself can work on primitives, but the call through the interface still goes through the boxed bridge.

Inline functions remove points 1 to 3 at the call site because no function object exists: the lambda body is pasted where it is used, working on primitives directly.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Not inline: every call goes through Function1<Integer, Integer>
fun applyTwice(x: Int, f: (Int) -> Int): Int = f(f(x))

// Inline: the lambda body is copied in, x stays a primitive int
inline fun applyTwiceInline(x: Int, f: (Int) -> Int): Int = f(f(x))

fun demo() {
    var sum = 0L
    for (i in 0 until 1_000_000) {
        sum += applyTwice(i) { it + 1000 }        // boxes args/results above 127
        sum += applyTwiceInline(i) { it + 1000 }  // no boxing, no Function1 object
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing "lambdas are free because the JVM optimizes them". The JIT helps, but allocation and boxing in hot loops still show up in allocation tracking, and ART's JIT/AOT profile is not HotSpot.
  • Forgetting the receiver is just the first parameter, so String.(Int) -> Unit and (String, Int) -> Unit are the same JVM type.
  • Thinking the 22-parameter limit still exists. It was lifted in Kotlin 1.3 via FunctionN, although a 23-parameter lambda is a design smell.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Java call a Kotlin (Int) -> Unit parameter? → It sees Function1<? super Integer, Unit> and must return Unit.INSTANCE, which is why Kotlin APIs meant for Java often use fun interface instead.
  2. Is there a way to avoid boxing without inline? → Use a fun interface IntOp { fun apply(x: Int): Int }. Its method is not generic, so it takes and returns a primitive int.
  3. Does boxing matter on modern ART? → In a one-off click handler, no. In per-frame or per-item code (draw, scroll, measure, 100k-element processing), yes. Measure with the Android Studio allocation tracker before and after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it becomes an object". The senior answer names Function1, explains erasure-driven boxing and the Integer cache range, separates allocation from dispatch cost, and gives the fun interface alternative for primitive-friendly, non-inline callbacks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom chart view called a (Float) -> Float mapper per point per frame. With 2,000 points at 60 fps that is 120k boxed Float allocations per second, and GC pauses showed up as jank. Making the mapper a fun interface with a primitive signature removed them.

questions.promptHtml: How do Kotlin lambdas compile to bytecode, and what changed in Kotlin 2.0?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you keep up with the compiler and know the practical side effects of a default change, not just "lambdas are objects".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Before Kotlin 2.0, each non-inline lambda became its own anonymous class extending kotlin.jvm.internal.Lambda and implementing FunctionN. Non-capturing ones were cached in a static INSTANCE field; capturing ones were allocated with the captured values as constructor fields. Since Kotlin 2.0, lambdas are compiled by default with invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory, the way Java compiles its lambdas: the body becomes a synthetic method on the enclosing class and the function object is created at runtime. That gives smaller binaries. The trade-offs listed in the 2.0 release notes: indy lambdas are not serializable, the experimental reflect() API does not work on them, and toString() is less readable. You can opt out per lambda with @JvmSerializableLambda or per module with -Xlambdas=class.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Old scheme (Kotlin 1.x default):

fun f() { val g = { x: Int -> x + 1 } }

-> class FooKt$f$g$1 extends kotlin.jvm.internal.Lambda implements Function1 {
       static final FooKt$f$g$1 INSTANCE = new FooKt$f$g$1();   // non-capturing only
       public final int invoke(int x) { return x + 1; }
       public Object invoke(Object x) { return invoke(((Number)x).intValue()); } // bridge
   }

One class per lambda. Lambda implements Serializable, and its toString() with kotlin-reflect printed the signature like (kotlin.Int) -> kotlin.Int.

New scheme (Kotlin 2.0+ default):

-> FooKt has: private static final int f$lambda$0(int x) { return x + 1; }
   call site: invokedynamic LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(... Function1.invoke ...)

No dedicated class in the Kotlin output. The JVM creates a hidden class at first execution.

Android detail: ART does not implement LambdaMetafactory. D8 desugars every invokedynamic lambda at build time into a small synthetic class (names like -$$ExternalSyntheticLambda0). So on Android the "smaller binary" comes from D8's synthetic classes being leaner than Kotlin's old classes (no Lambda superclass, no arity bookkeeping), not from runtime spinning. D8 has done this for Java 8 lambdas for years, so it is a well-tested path.

What actually changed for app code:

Behavior 1.x class lambdas 2.0 indy lambdas
Class count in Kotlin output 1 per lambda 0 (synthetic method instead)
is java.io.Serializable true false
toString() readable signature (with kotlin-reflect) FooKt$$Lambda$13/0x...@hash-style, on Android a D8 synthetic name
reflect() (experimental) works not supported
Opt-out n/a @JvmSerializableLambda on a lambda, or -Xlambdas=class for the module

Inline lambdas are unaffected because no function object exists. Suspend lambdas still compile as classes (they need a state machine; chunk 13).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.io.Serializable

fun main() {
    val plain = { println("hi") }
    println(plain is Serializable)        // Kotlin 2.0 default: false (1.9: true)

    val keep = @JvmSerializableLambda { println("hi") }
    println(keep is Serializable)         // true: compiled the old way
}
// build.gradle.kts, module-wide opt-out (only if you truly depend on old behavior)
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.add("-Xlambdas=class")
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a lambda's toString() or class name as a key (analytics, de-duplication, logging). It silently changed with 2.0.
  • Relying on lambdas being Serializable (passing one through a Bundle). Q090 is a production version of this.
  • Assuming -Xlambdas=class is the fix. It is a compatibility switch; the real fix is to not serialize or stringify lambdas.
  • Thinking indy lambdas are slower on Android. After D8 desugaring they are ordinary classes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do capturing lambdas allocate in both schemes? → Yes. Each evaluation of a capturing lambda creates a new object holding the captured values. Only non-capturing lambdas are cached.
  2. Which flag gave indy before 2.0? → -Xlambdas=indy, available since Kotlin 1.5.
  3. How would you verify which scheme a module uses? → Look at the bytecode (Android Studio "Show Kotlin Bytecode", or javap -c on the class) for invokedynamic versus a $1 lambda class, or check the dex with APK Analyzer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "lambdas become anonymous classes" (true in 2019). The senior answer knows the 2.0 default switched to invokedynamic, knows D8 desugars it on Android, and lists the three behavioral differences plus the two opt-outs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Upgrades to Kotlin 2.0 surfaced code that persisted lambdas or used lambda.toString() as a map key. Neither showed up as a compile error.

questions.promptHtml: Java lambdas can only capture effectively final variables. Kotlin lambdas can modify a captured var. How does that work, and what are the consequences?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you understand closures as heap objects, and whether you spot the threading and lifetime consequences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When a non-inline lambda captures a local var and the variable is modified, the compiler moves it to the heap: it wraps it in kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref.IntRef, ObjectRef and similar, with a single mutable field element. Both the function and the lambda share that box, so a write in one is seen by the other. Consequences: an extra allocation, the lambda sees the latest value and not the value at capture time, and the field is a plain non-volatile field, so sharing it across threads is a data race. For inline lambdas there is no box, because the body is in the same frame.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
fun counter(): () -> Int {
    var count = 0
    return { ++count }
}

Compiled (shape):
    Ref.IntRef count = new Ref.IntRef();   // heap box
    count.element = 0;
    return new Lambda(count);              // lambda holds the box
    // lambda.invoke(): return ++count.element;

Rules:

  • val captured: the value is copied into the lambda object. No box needed.
  • var captured and never modified after capture: the compiler still treats it as a var; it may box it. Do not count on optimizations; make it val if it does not change.
  • var captured by an inline lambda: no box. The code runs in the caller's frame and reads the local directly.
  • Ref types: IntRef, LongRef, BooleanRef, FloatRef, DoubleRef, CharRef, ByteRef, ShortRef, ObjectRef<T>.

Semantics that bite:

  1. Late binding. The lambda reads the current value when it runs, not the value when it was created.
  2. No thread safety. element is a normal field. Two threads doing count.element++ lose updates, and one thread may not see another's write without a happens-before edge. Use AtomicInteger or confinement (chunk 21 owns synchronization).
  3. Lifetime. The box lives as long as the longest-living lambda that captured it.

Loop nuance: for (i in 0 until n) declares a fresh val i per iteration, so each lambda captures its own value. A var declared outside a while loop is a single shared box, so every lambda sees the final value.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun buildHandlers(n: Int): List<() -> Int> {
    val fresh = (0 until n).map { i -> { i } }   // each captures its own i: 0,1,2

    var index = 0
    val shared = mutableListOf<() -> Int>()
    while (index < n) {
        shared += { index }                     // all share one IntRef
        index++
    }
    // fresh.map { it() } == [0, 1, 2]; shared.map { it() } == [3, 3, 3] for n = 3
    return fresh + shared
}

// Correct fix for the shared case: copy into a val at capture time
fun buildHandlersFixed(n: Int): List<() -> Int> {
    var index = 0
    val out = mutableListOf<() -> Int>()
    while (index < n) {
        val captured = index
        out += { captured }
        index++
    }
    return out
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutating a captured var from a callback that runs on a background thread and reading it on main. It looks like Java's "effectively final" rule was relaxed for free; it was not made thread-safe.
  • Expecting capture-time values in while loops or when the var is reassigned after the lambda is created.
  • Capturing a large object in a long-lived lambda by accident (for example this of an Activity through a member access). The lambda object holds it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does capturing this work the same way? → Accessing a member property or function captures the enclosing instance (this), not a copy of the field. The lambda then keeps the whole object alive. Chunk 06 covers the Activity leak scenario.
  2. Is IntRef marked volatile? → No. It is a plain field; visibility across threads needs synchronization or an atomic.
  3. Why does an inline lambda not need IntRef? → Its body is copied into the caller's method, so it accesses the local variable slot directly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "Kotlin allows it". The senior answer explains the Ref box, late binding, the race, and the zero-cost inline case, and knows the copy-into-val fix.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics helper counted impressions with a captured var count incremented from an image-loading callback on a background pool. Counts were 3 to 5 percent low under fast scrolling because of lost updates.

questions.promptHtml: What does the inline modifier do, and why does the standard library use it for functions like let, forEach and repeat?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most asked Kotlin question in this area. They want the mechanism (copying bytecode), not "it makes things faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When a function is inline, the compiler copies its body into every call site, and also copies the bodies of the lambdas passed to it. So no function object is created for those lambdas, nothing is boxed, and there is no extra call. Inlining also enables things normal lambdas cannot do: non-local return from the caller, reified type parameters, and calling suspend functions inside the lambda when the caller is suspend. The cost is bigger bytecode at each call site, so it pays off mainly for small functions that take function-type parameters.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Source:
    inline fun measure(block: () -> Unit): Long {
        val start = System.nanoTime()
        block()
        return System.nanoTime() - start
    }
    fun load() { val t = measure { parse() } }

After inlining, load() is compiled as if you wrote:
    fun load() {
        val start = System.nanoTime()
        parse()
        val t = System.nanoTime() - start
    }

No Function0, no allocation, no invoke call.

What inlining gives you:

Benefit Why it needs inline
No lambda object or boxing body copied, no FunctionN needed
Non-local return lambda body lives in the caller's frame (Q082)
reified T the real type argument is known at each copied call site (Q085)
Suspend calls inside the lambda the body is part of the caller's suspend function
Labeled break/continue out of the lambda supported as non-local break/continue in newer Kotlin (chunk 11 tracks version status)

What it costs:

  • Bytecode grows by the function's size times the number of call sites.
  • Public inline functions become part of your ABI (Q086).
  • Inline functions cannot be recursive, and public ones cannot touch private or internal declarations (except @PublishedApi internal).

The compiler warns (NOTHING_TO_INLINE) when an inline function has no function-type parameters and no reified type: "expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant". The JIT already inlines small normal calls.

Inline also applies to property accessors without backing fields: inline val View.isVisibleNow: Boolean get() = visibility == View.VISIBLE.

The inline function itself still exists as a normal method in bytecode (so Java and reflection can call it), except that functions with reified parameters cannot be called that way.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Good inline candidate: small, takes a lambda, called often
inline fun <T> List<T>.sumByLong(selector: (T) -> Long): Long {
    var sum = 0L
    for (item in this) sum += selector(item)
    return sum
}

// Pointless inline: no function-type params, compiler warns NOTHING_TO_INLINE
inline fun square(x: Int) = x * x   // just make it a normal fun

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Marking everything inline "for performance". Without lambda parameters it only grows code.
  • Thinking inline means "runs on another thread" or "runs lazily". It runs exactly where it is called, synchronously.
  • Assuming a lambda stored in a variable and then passed to an inline function avoids allocation. The object already exists; inlining only removes the call.
  • Forgetting that the inlined code is part of the caller: an exception stack trace points at the inline function's file and line through SMAP mapping, which can confuse people reading crash reports.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an inline function call itself? → No, direct recursion is a compile error. The expansion would never end.
  2. Why are let, apply and forEach inline? → They exist only to run a lambda. Without inline every ?.let {} would allocate, and you could not return from the outer function inside forEach.
  3. Does the debugger stop inside inlined code? → Yes. The compiler emits source-mapping (SMAP) info, and since Kotlin 1.x the debugger can step into inline lambdas, although local variable display can be odd.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it avoids creating lambda objects". The senior answer adds the four capabilities (non-local return, reified, suspend in lambdas, no boxing), the NOTHING_TO_INLINE warning, and that the cost is code size and ABI coupling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams sometimes ban inline after one bad experience with method count, then find measureTimeMillis-style helpers allocating in hot paths. The rule is "inline small helpers that take lambdas", not "never" or "always".

questions.promptHtml: Explain non-local returns. What do return, return@label and return inside an anonymous function each do in Kotlin?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The forEach { return } behavior is a top source of logic bugs. Interviewers want you to predict control flow exactly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bare return always returns from the nearest enclosing fun. Inside a lambda passed to an inline function, that fun is the outer function, so the return leaves the whole function: that is a non-local return. return@label returns only from the lambda labeled label; the implicit label is the name of the function the lambda was passed to, like return@forEach. An anonymous function, fun(x: Int) { ... }, is a real function, so a bare return inside it returns only from itself. In forEach, return@forEach acts like continue, not break.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
fun find(items: List<Int>): String {
    items.forEach {
        if (it < 0) return "negative found"     // (1) leaves find()
        if (it == 0) return@forEach             // (2) skips to next item, like continue
    }
    items.forEach loop@{
        if (it == 99) return@loop               // (3) explicit label, same as (2)
    }
    items.forEach(fun(x) {
        if (x == 42) return                     // (4) leaves the anonymous fun only
    })
    run outer@{
        items.forEach { if (it > 10) return@outer }  // (5) "break" out of forEach
    }
    return "ok"
}

Rules:

  • Non-local return is allowed only from lambdas passed to inline function parameters that are not noinline or crossinline.
  • return@label with a value: list.map { if (it == 0) return@map -1; it * 2 }.
  • Labels are name@ before the lambda; return@name jumps there.
  • To emulate break in forEach, wrap in run outer@{ } and return@outer, or just use a for loop. The for loop is clearer.
  • break and continue inside an inline lambda targeting an outer loop: this is the "non-local break and continue" feature added in the Kotlin 2.x line (preview in 2.1, stable in 2.2 per the "What's new" pages; chunk 11 tracks status). On older versions it does not compile.

Why does it work? An inline lambda's body is copied into the outer function. A return in it becomes an ordinary return instruction of the outer method. A non-inline lambda compiles to a separate invoke method, where "return from the outer function" has no meaning.

Inline functions with try/finally still run their finally on a non-local return, because the return goes through the finally block in the same method. Inline functions that do cleanup without finally skip it (Q089).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun firstInvalid(emails: List<String>): String? {
    emails.forEach { email ->
        if (email.isBlank()) return@forEach          // skip blanks, keep looping
        if ('@' !in email) return email              // found it: leave the function
    }
    return null
}

// Clearer than any label trick when you need break:
fun firstInvalidLoop(emails: List<String>): String? {
    for (email in emails) {
        if (email.isBlank()) continue
        if ('@' !in email) return email
    }
    return null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing return in forEach intending continue. It ends the function, and code after the loop never runs.
  • Expecting return@forEach to break the loop. It only finishes the current iteration.
  • Using return inside list.map { } and getting a non-local return from the outer function instead of a mapped value.
  • Assuming every "forEach-like" API allows non-local return. Sequence.forEach does (it is inline), but Flow.collect {} does not: its lambda becomes a FlowCollector (a non-inline suspend callback), so a bare return does not compile. Use return@collect to skip, or stop early with first {} / takeWhile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When would you pick an anonymous function over a lambda? → When the body has several early returns that should exit only the callback, or when you want an explicit return type. fun(x): Boolean { ... } reads better than many return@filter.
  2. Does a non-local return inside synchronized {} release the lock? → Yes. stdlib synchronized is inline and releases the monitor in a finally, so returns and exceptions both unlock.
  3. Can a crossinline lambda use return@label? → Yes, local returns are always fine. Only bare non-local return is forbidden.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows "return in forEach returns from the function". The senior answer explains why (body copied into the caller frame), uses anonymous functions where labels get ugly, knows return@forEach is continue, and prefers a for loop when break semantics are needed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout validator used items.forEach { if (it.qty == 0) return } to "skip" zero items. Every cart with a zero-quantity line skipped the stock check that came after the loop. See Q087 for the full scenario.

questions.promptHtml: What is noinline, when are you forced to use it, and what do you lose when you add it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you understand that an inlined lambda is not an object, and what that means for storing or forwarding it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In an inline function, every function-type parameter is inlined by default, which means it is not a real object: I cannot store it in a field, put it in a list, or pass it to a non-inline function. If I need to do any of that with one parameter, I mark that parameter noinline. That parameter then becomes a normal lambda object with allocation and possibly boxing, and it loses non-local return, while the other parameters stay inlined. If every lambda parameter ends up noinline, the function should not be inline at all.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An inlined parameter only exists as code to paste. The compiler allows you to call it (block()) or pass it on to another inline function's inlined parameter. Anything that treats it as a value is an error:

inline fun register(onEvent: () -> Unit) {
    listeners.add(onEvent)        // ERROR: Illegal usage of inline-parameter 'onEvent'
    val f = onEvent               // ERROR
    Handler(looper).post(onEvent) // ERROR (passed to a non-inline Java method)
}

With noinline:

inline fun register(noinline onEvent: () -> Unit, filter: (Event) -> Boolean) {
    if (filter(currentEvent)) {   // filter: still inlined, called directly
        listeners.add(onEvent)    // OK: onEvent is a normal Function0 object
    }
}
inlined parameter noinline parameter
Is a runtime object no yes (Function0 etc.)
Can be stored / forwarded to non-inline code no yes
Non-local return inside it yes no
Allocation per call none yes if capturing
Can call suspend functions inside (when caller is suspend) yes only if its type is suspend () -> Unit

Typical reasons for a mixed signature: a function that inlines a hot predicate but stores a completion callback, or one that needs reified T (forcing inline) while also passing a callback to a non-inline API.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.view.View

// reified forces inline; the click callback must be stored by the View, so noinline
inline fun <reified T : View> View.onChildClick(
    id: Int,
    noinline action: (T) -> Unit,
) {
    val child = findViewById<T>(id)
    child.setOnClickListener { action(it as T) }   // listener lambda captures action
}

// Smell: everything noinline and no reified -> just remove inline
inline fun schedule(noinline a: () -> Unit, noinline b: () -> Unit) { /* ... */ }

Note: in onChildClick, setOnClickListener { action(...) } creates a non-inline lambda that captures action. Using action there requires it to be a value, which is why it is noinline. An alternative is crossinline (Q084), which keeps it inlinable into that inner lambda's body; which one is right depends on whether you need the object itself.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding noinline to silence an error without asking whether the function should be inline at all.
  • Expecting non-local return inside a noinline lambda. It does not compile.
  • Not realizing noinline brings back the allocation the caller thought inline removed.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference between noinline and crossinline in one line? → noinline makes it a real object you can store; crossinline keeps it inlined but forbids non-local return because it will run inside another lambda or object.
  2. Can a noinline parameter be nullable? → Yes, and it must be: an inlined function-type parameter cannot be nullable. inline fun f(noinline cb: (() -> Unit)? = null) is a common pattern.
  3. Does noinline affect the other parameters? → No, it is per parameter.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "noinline means don't inline this lambda". The senior answer names the exact operations that force it (store, forward to non-inline code, nullable), the capabilities lost, and the rule that an inline function with only noinline parameters and no reified type should not be inline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Code review catches inline functions where every parameter got noinline over time. They still bloat each call site with the wrapper body but give none of the benefits.

questions.promptHtml: Why does crossinline exist? Show the compile error it solves and explain what it guarantees.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Very few candidates can explain it beyond "it prevents non-local returns". The senior signal is knowing why that would be unsafe.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Sometimes an inline function does not call its lambda directly but inside another lambda or an object, like a Runnable, a listener, or a flow {} block. That inner context runs later, possibly after the outer function has returned. If the caller's lambda contained a non-local return, there would be no frame to return to. So the compiler refuses unless I mark the parameter crossinline. crossinline keeps the lambda inlined into that inner body, so I still avoid a separate lambda object for it, but forbids non-local returns from the caller's lambda.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
inline fun runLater(block: () -> Unit) {
    handler.post { block() }
}
// ERROR: Can't inline 'block' here: it may contain non-local returns.
//        Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'block'.

Why: the { block() } passed to post is a normal non-inline lambda (a Runnable). If block were inlined into it and contained return, that return would try to leave the caller of runLater, which may have finished long ago.

With crossinline:

inline fun runLater(crossinline block: () -> Unit) {
    handler.post { block() }   // block's body is copied into the Runnable's run()
}

fun onSave() {
    runLater {
        save()
        return        // ERROR now: 'return' is not allowed here
        return@runLater   // OK: local return
    }
}

What actually happens in bytecode: the Runnable is still one object, created per call (it is generated at each call site because its body contains the caller's code). block itself is not a separate object. So crossinline saves one allocation versus noinline, but the inner object still exists.

Where you see it in real APIs:

  • Flow operators written as inline fun <T, R> Flow<T>.map(crossinline transform: suspend (T) -> R): Flow<R> = transform { value -> emit(transform(value)) }. The transform runs inside a collector lambda that runs later.
  • inline fun <reified T> Context.startActivity(crossinline configure: Intent.() -> Unit)-style helpers when the lambda is called inside a nested block.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.os.Handler
import android.os.Looper

private val main = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())

inline fun postToMain(crossinline block: () -> Unit) {
    main.post { block() }          // inlined into the Runnable body
}

fun refreshUi(isReady: Boolean) {
    postToMain {
        if (!isReady) return@postToMain   // local return: fine
        render()
    }
}

fun render() {}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking crossinline removes all allocation. The wrapping lambda or object is still created per call.
  • Thinking crossinline means "runs on another thread". It only says the lambda is invoked from a different execution context; the thread is whatever that context uses.
  • Using noinline when crossinline would do. noinline adds a second object (the lambda) on top of the wrapper.
  • Missing that a crossinline lambda can still be called after the outer function returns, so captured state must be valid then.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a crossinline lambda call suspend functions? → Only if its type is a suspend function type, for example crossinline transform: suspend (T) -> R as in Flow operators. A plain crossinline block: () -> Unit used inside a Runnable cannot suspend, because the Runnable is not a suspend context.
  2. Is crossinline needed when the inline function passes the lambda to another inline function's normal parameter? → No. Inline-into-inline keeps the same frame, so non-local return is still safe.
  3. When do you prefer noinline over crossinline? → When you need the lambda as an object (store it, compare it, pass it to non-inline code by reference). crossinline only lets you call it inside the nested body.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "crossinline disables non-local returns". The senior answer explains the missing-frame problem, shows the exact compiler error, notes that the wrapper object is still allocated, and points to Flow's operator implementations as the canonical use.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Chunk 06 has a full scenario on a crossinline lambda posted in a Runnable and the lifetime bugs that follow. The core lesson: crossinline code runs later, so treat it like any deferred callback.

questions.promptHtml: What does reified do, why does it only work on inline functions, and what are its limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: inline fun <reified T> is everywhere in Android code (viewModels<VM>(), getParcelableExtra, DI lookups, JSON helpers). They check that you understand erasure and the mechanism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On the JVM, generic type arguments are erased, so inside a normal fun <T> I cannot do T::class, is T or as T safely. A reified type parameter fixes that at compile time: because the function is inline, the compiler copies its body into each call site and substitutes the actual type there, so T::class becomes String::class at one call and User::class at another. That is why it only works with inline. Limits: the caller must know a concrete type (or itself have a reified T), Java cannot call such functions, and nested generics are still erased below the top level, for example List<User> becomes just List.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA(): Boolean = this is T

call: x.isA<String>()
after inlining: x is String

The compiler emits the concrete class in the copied bytecode. Nothing is passed at runtime.

What you can do with reified T:

Use Example
Class literal T::class, T::class.java
Type check / cast x is T, x as T, filterIsInstance<T>()
Array creation arrayOf<T>() / arrayOfNulls<T>(n) works with reified T
Full type with generics typeOf<T>() gives a KType that includes arguments like List<User>

Limits:

  1. Only in inline functions, and T must be marked reified.
  2. Caller needs a concrete type. From fun <T> wrap() = parse<T>() you get "Cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead." The chain must be reified all the way up.
  3. Java callers get a method that throws UnsupportedOperationException ("This function has a reified type parameter and thus can only be inlined at compilation time, not called directly").
  4. Nested generics. T::class.java for T = List<User> is List.class; the User part is lost. Use typeOf<T>() (kotlin.reflect, stable since 1.6) when a library needs the full type, as kotlinx.serialization's serializer<T>() does. Gson's TypeToken story lives in chunk 08.
  5. Cannot be used on classes, only on functions (and inline properties' type parameters).
  6. Code size: each call site gets its own copy, so large reified functions multiply bytecode.

The common pattern for keeping reified functions small is a thin inline wrapper over a non-inline function that takes a Class<T> or KType:

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import android.content.Intent
import android.os.Build
import android.os.Parcelable

// Thin reified wrapper, real work in a non-inline function
inline fun <reified T : Parcelable> Intent.parcelable(key: String): T? =
    parcelableImpl(key, T::class.java)

@PublishedApi
internal fun <T : Parcelable> Intent.parcelableImpl(key: String, clazz: Class<T>): T? =
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 33) getParcelableExtra(key, clazz)
    else @Suppress("DEPRECATION") getParcelableExtra(key)

// Broken: T is not reified, so no class information exists
// fun <T> Intent.broken(key: String): T? = parcelable<T>(key) // compile error

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting T::class to include generic arguments. It does not; use typeOf<T>() when you need them.
  • Writing a big reified function used in hundreds of places. Delegate to a non-inline worker taking Class<T>.
  • Exposing reified helpers as a library's only API, then Java consumers cannot use them. Provide a Class<T> overload.
  • Assuming as T in a non-reified generic function checks anything. It is an unchecked cast that fails later, somewhere else.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does by viewModels<MyVm>() know the class? → It is an inline function with a reified VM, and it uses VM::class to build the lazy ViewModel lookup.
  2. Why is the worker function @PublishedApi internal? → A public inline function's body is copied into other modules, so everything it calls must be public ABI. @PublishedApi makes an internal declaration callable from inlined code while keeping it out of normal autocompletion (Q086).
  3. Can I use reified to get a T instance? → Not directly. You have the class, so you can reflectively call a constructor (T::class.java.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()), but that is reflection with all its costs and R8 keep-rule needs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "reified lets you access T at runtime". The senior answer says "at compile time, per call site, by inlining", lists the limits (Java, chains, nested generics, code size), and shows the thin-wrapper plus @PublishedApi pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reified inline fun <reified T> fromJson(s: String): T built with T::class.java worked for User but returned List<LinkedTreeMap> for List<User>, crashing later with ClassCastException in a RecyclerView adapter. The fix was passing the full type (typeOf<T>() or a TypeToken).

questions.subtopic: When NOT to inline (code size, public API & ABI)
questions.promptHtml: When should you not make a function inline? Talk about code size and about publishing public inline functions in a library.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers own APIs and binaries. This shows whether you know that inline turns implementation details into contracts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I skip inline when the function has no function-type parameters and no reified type, when its body is large and it is called from many places, when I need recursion, or when the lambda must be stored anyway. For public library APIs I am careful because the body of a public inline function gets copied into the consumer's compiled code. Changing that body does not reach consumers until they recompile, everything it calls has to be public or @PublishedApi internal, and renaming or removing those helpers breaks already-compiled consumers with NoSuchMethodError. So a public inline function is part of my binary ABI, not just my source API.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decision table:

Situation Inline?
Small function, takes a lambda, called in hot or many paths (measure {}, withLock {}) yes
Needs reified T yes, but keep the inline part thin
Needs non-local return or suspend calls in the lambda from non-suspend helper signatures yes
No function-type params, no reified no (NOTHING_TO_INLINE warning)
Large body (say 50+ lines) called from 200 sites no, or split into thin inline + non-inline worker
Lambda is stored or forwarded probably no (it becomes noinline anyway)
Recursive cannot
Public API of a library with independent release cadence only if the body is tiny and stable

Code size math: an inline function whose body compiles to about 120 bytes of bytecode, called from 300 sites, adds roughly 300 x 120 = 36 KB of bytecode before R8, versus 120 bytes once plus 300 small call instructions. R8 can shrink some of it, but it cannot un-inline. Inline lambdas also pass their bodies into the copies, which is expected; the wrapper overhead is the part you multiply.

ABI rules for public inline functions:

  1. Body is copied into consumers. If library A v1.0 ships inline fun log(msg: () -> String) { if (enabled) println(msg()) } and v1.1 fixes a bug in it, any already-compiled library B that inlined v1.0 keeps the v1.0 behavior even when the app upgrades A to 1.1. Only recompiling B picks up the fix.
  2. Visibility. A public inline function cannot access private or internal members: "Public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API". The escape hatch is @PublishedApi internal, which makes the declaration effectively public in bytecode.
  3. @PublishedApi declarations are ABI. Renaming or changing their signature breaks precompiled consumers at runtime with NoSuchMethodError or NoSuchFieldError, even though they look internal in source.
  4. Tooling. The Kotlin binary-compatibility-validator Gradle plugin dumps the public ABI (including @PublishedApi) into an .api file and fails the build on unintentional changes. Newer Kotlin Gradle plugin versions also ship an experimental built-in ABI validation; check your version's docs before relying on it.

Inside an app (single Gradle build), point 1 mostly does not hurt, because all modules recompile together. It matters for SDKs, prebuilt AARs, and dynamic feature modules built separately.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Library module: keep the inline surface tiny and stable
public inline fun traceSection(name: String, block: () -> Unit) {
    val token = Tracer.begin(name)     // public, stable API
    try { block() } finally { Tracer.end(token) }
}

// Helpers called from public inline code must be public ABI
@PublishedApi
internal fun internalLogImpl(tag: String, msg: String) { /* ... */ }

public inline fun debugLog(tag: String, msg: () -> String) {
    if (Logger.enabled) internalLogImpl(tag, msg())
}

object Tracer {
    fun begin(name: String): Int = 0
    fun end(token: Int) {}
}
object Logger { @JvmField var enabled = false }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating @PublishedApi internal as private. It is binary public; consumers' inlined bytecode calls it by name.
  • Shipping a "hotfix" inside a public inline function and expecting it to reach all users. It reaches only code compiled after the upgrade.
  • Inlining a big function to "save a call". The JIT/AOT already inlines small hot calls; you gain little and pay in size.
  • Making a reified function huge instead of delegating to a Class<T> worker.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you change a public inline function's behavior safely? → Keep the inline body a thin call into a non-inline function, and change that function. The inlined code then calls the new logic at runtime.
  2. Does R8 help with inline bloat? → It removes dead code and can optimize, but it does not undo source-level inlining. Measure with APK Analyzer or method count diffs.
  3. Can you deprecate a public inline function? → Yes, with @Deprecated and a ReplaceWith, but keep it and its @PublishedApi helpers binary-present until consumers have recompiled, often a full major version.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "do not inline large functions". The senior answer explains that public inline bodies are copied into consumers (so fixes do not propagate and @PublishedApi helpers are frozen ABI), uses the thin-inline-plus-worker pattern, and puts binary-compatibility-validator in CI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Q092 is a post-incident review of exactly this: an SDK fixed a bug inside a public inline function, but a prebuilt partner AAR kept the old inlined body, and a later rename of a @PublishedApi helper crashed it with NoSuchMethodError.

questions.contextHtml:
An e-commerce app (1.2M DAU) shows "Out of stock" errors only after payment, about 0.4 percent of orders, rising since a refactor two weeks ago. Backend logs show those orders were sent without a stock check token. QA cannot reproduce with normal carts. Crashlytics is clean. A teammate suspects a race in the stock API (red herring: the API p95 latency did go from 180 ms to 260 ms the same week). The refactored validator:

suspend fun validateCart(cart: Cart): ValidationResult {
    cart.items.forEach { item ->
        if (item.quantity == 0) return ValidationResult.Ok   // "skip removed lines"
        if (item.price < 0) return ValidationResult.Error("bad price")
    }
    val token = stockApi.reserve(cart.items.filter { it.quantity > 0 })
    return ValidationResult.Ok.withToken(token)
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it only hits some orders, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The stock API is slow, add a retry or a timeout" or "make the reserve call before the loop". They chase the latency red herring and do not read the return inside forEach.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Can a cart contain zero-quantity lines? (If the UI keeps "removed" items with quantity 0 for an undo feature, this matters.)
    • What fraction of affected orders contain a zero-quantity line? That is the direct test of my hypothesis.
    • What exactly changed in the refactor diff? Was this previously a for loop with continue?
    • Does ValidationResult.Ok without a token get accepted by checkout? Apparently yes, which is a second bug.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the backend reject orders without a stock token (server-side guard), or flip a remote config to force the old validation path if one exists. That stops bad orders while the client fix rolls out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) return inside forEach is a non-local return: it exits validateCart on the first zero-quantity item, returning Ok without reserving stock. Matches "only some orders" and "no token".
    • (b) Stock API race under higher latency. Would cause failures with a token present, not missing tokens.
    • (c) Cancellation of validateCart mid-flight. Would surface as a cancelled flow, not an Ok result.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • For (a): query affected orders for zero-quantity lines; I expect close to 100 percent. Write a unit test with runTest and a fake stockApi that records calls: cart [qty 0, qty 2] should call reserve once; it calls it zero times.
    • For (b): compare server logs for reserve calls on affected orders. None exist, which rules it out.
    • For (c): coroutine debug logs or Crashlytics non-fatals for CancellationException in checkout. Nothing.
  5. Root cause: forEach is an inline function, so the lambda body is pasted into validateCart. A bare return there is a return from validateCart itself. The author meant "skip this item" (continue). The first zero-quantity line ends validation with Ok and the reserve call is never reached. Carts with zero-quantity lines come from the new "undo remove" feature, which is why only some orders are affected.
  6. Fix: Short-term: 
    suspend fun validateCart(cart: Cart): ValidationResult {
    for (item in cart.items) {
        if (item.quantity == 0) continue
        if (item.price < 0) return ValidationResult.Error("bad price")
    }
    val token = stockApi.reserve(cart.items.filter { it.quantity > 0 })
    return ValidationResult.Ok.withToken(token)
}
    (return@forEach would also work, but a for loop makes "continue" and "return" unambiguous.) Long-term: make Ok require a token at the type level (data class Ok(val token: StockToken)), so an "Ok without token" cannot be constructed, and keep the server-side check.
  7. Prevention:
    • Unit tests for validators with zero-quantity, negative-price and empty carts.
    • A review checklist item: "bare return inside a lambda" gets a second look. Detekt has rules in this area (for example around labeled expressions); a custom lint rule that flags bare return inside forEach in validation code is cheap.
    • Server-side invariant: no stock token, no order.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add retries or timeouts to the stock API; that treats a symptom that does not exist. I would not ban forEach globally; the problem is non-local return, and a team rule "use for when you need control flow" is enough.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the code used items.asSequence().forEach? → Same bug. Sequence.forEach is also inline.
  • What if it used items.stream().forEach { ... return ... } (Java stream)? → It would not compile; Java's forEach takes a Consumer, which is not inlined, so a bare return is not allowed. The compiler would have caught it.
  • Would return@forEach ValidationResult.Ok compile? → No. forEach's lambda returns Unit, so a labeled return with a value is a type error. That error would have been a hint.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a payments team, a refactor from for loops to forEach "for style" turned two continues into returns. Tests only covered single-item carts. We added a property-based test that shuffles carts with zero-quantity items, and it failed on the first run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the API latency, cannot explain what return does inside forEach.
  • Hire: identifies the non-local return, fixes with for/continue or return@forEach, adds a test.
  • Strong hire: explains why inline makes it non-local, connects the 0.4 percent to the undo feature, adds a type-level guarantee and a server-side check, and dismisses the red herring with evidence.

questions.contextHtml:
A news feed (400k DAU) renders horizontal carousels of up to 10 cards inside a feed RecyclerView; each carousel is a plain LinearLayout filled in code. After release 7.4, the analytics team reports that 60 percent of carousel taps are attributed to "position 10", which does not exist (positions are 0 to 9), and the last card's CTR jumped 4x. The change: a developer replaced a for (i in cards.indices) loop with a while loop "to prepare for pagination". Logs from a tester tapping the first card:

D/Analytics: carousel_tap id=card_9 position=10 visible=[0,1,2]
D/Analytics: carousel_tap id=card_9 position=10 visible=[0,1,2]

Red herring: the same release bumped RecyclerView and moved the feed adapter to ListAdapter. The code:

fun bindCarousel(cards: List<Card>, container: ViewGroup) {
    var index = 0
    var current = cards.firstOrNull() ?: return
    while (index < cards.size) {
        current = cards[index]
        val view = inflateCard(container, current)
        view.setOnClickListener {

    }
}

Support tickets say "tapping a story opens a different story, but only sometimes". About 40 percent of carousels are single-card sponsored units.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening, why it looked intermittent, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "RecyclerView recycles views so the listener is stale; call notifyDataSetChanged." They blame the library bump and never notice that all listeners share one variable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is "sometimes" correlated with carousel size? Single-card carousels would look correct under my hypothesis.
    • Did attribution break exactly in 7.4? Version filter in analytics.
    • Are taps on the first card ever attributed correctly? If never, it is deterministic, not a race.
    • Is cards a snapshot or a list that pagination mutates? It decides whether capturing an index is ever safe here.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Analytics is wrong but the "opens wrong card" bug hurts users. Ship a hotfix (it is a two-line change) and mark analytics from the affected versions as untrustworthy in the dashboard.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The click lambda captures the local vars index and current. Because they are modified after capture, the compiler boxes them in shared Ref.IntRef / Ref.ObjectRef objects. Every listener in one carousel reads the same boxes, which hold cards.size and the last card after the loop.
    • (b) RecyclerView recycling binds stale listeners. Would mix positions across carousels, not converge on "last card, position 10".
    • (c) Analytics SDK batching reorders events. Would not change the position field value.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • (a): decompile with "Show Kotlin Bytecode" and see Ref.IntRef and Ref.ObjectRef passed into the listener. A Robolectric test that binds 3 cards and clicks the first one reproduces it every time.
    • (b): the cards live in a plain LinearLayout, not a nested RecyclerView, so recycling does not touch these listeners.
    • (c): local logcat already shows the wrong value before the SDK.
  5. Root cause: Kotlin lets a lambda capture a mutable local by moving it into a heap box (Ref.IntRef, Ref.ObjectRef). All listeners created in the loop share those boxes, and each listener reads them when the tap happens, not when it was created. By then the loop has finished: index == cards.size (10) and current is the last card. So every tap opens the last card and logs position 10. It looked intermittent because single-card carousels (40 percent) and taps on the last card behave correctly by coincidence. The old for (i in cards.indices) loop declared a fresh val i per iteration, so it was safe.
  6. Fix: 
    fun bindCarousel(cards: List<Card>, container: ViewGroup) {
    cards.forEachIndexed { position, card ->      // fresh vals per iteration
        val view = inflateCard(container, card)
        view.setOnClickListener {
            analytics.track("carousel_tap", card.id, position)
            openCard(card)
        }
        container.addView(view)
    }
}
    Capture the Card itself, not an index into a list that may change. Long-term: move the carousel to a RecyclerView with a stable-ID ListAdapter and resolve the item at click time with bindingAdapterPosition, checking RecyclerView.NO_POSITION.
  7. Prevention:
    • Review rule: a lambda that will run later (listener, callback, post) should capture vals only. Capturing a var is a smell worth a comment.
    • A UI test that taps the first and last carousel cards and asserts the opened ID.
    • Analytics validation dashboards that alert on impossible distributions (one position over 3x the average CTR).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not "fix" it by reading index - 1 or clamping. I would not roll back the RecyclerView bump; it is unrelated, and rolling it back costs another release cycle without fixing anything.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would Java have caught this? → Yes. Java requires captured locals to be effectively final, so index++ after capture would not compile. Kotlin trades that safety for convenience.
  • What if the callback ran on a background thread and also incremented index? → Now you also have a data race: IntRef.element is a plain field, not volatile. Use an AtomicInteger or confine to one thread.
  • Does for (i in 0 until n) have the same problem? → No. Each iteration declares a new val i, so each lambda captures its own value.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "pagination-friendly" refactor turned every for loop in a feed module into while loops with a shared counter. Three screens had the same capture bug. We added a Detekt custom rule that flags lambdas passed to setOnClickListener/post capturing a local var, and it found two more.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames RecyclerView or the analytics SDK; does not know Kotlin can capture vars.
  • Hire: identifies the shared captured var, fixes with per-iteration vals or forEachIndexed.
  • Strong hire: explains the Ref boxes and late binding, explains the "sometimes" through single-card carousels, captures the item instead of an index, and adds a test plus a review rule.

A notes app (2M DAU, 35 percent low-end devices) saw ANR rate rise from 0.18 percent to 0.9 percent over a week after release 5.2. The ANR traces in Play Console all look like this:

"main" prio=5 tid=1 Waiting
  at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native method)
  at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(LockSupport.java:211)
  at java.util.concurrent.locks.AbstractQueuedSynchronizer.acquire(...)
  at java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock.lock(ReentrantLock.java:322)
  at com.app.notes.NoteCache.get(NoteCache.kt:41)

The same release upgraded Room (red herring: Room's own threads are idle in the traces). Perfetto traces from internal dogfood also show NoteCache#sync sections that never end. 5.2 introduced this helper, used in 14 places:

inline fun <T> ReentrantLock.guarded(section: String, block: () -> T): T {
    Trace.beginSection(section)
    lock()
    val result = block()
    unlock()
    Trace.endSection()
    return result
}

class NoteCache(private val lock: ReentrantLock = ReentrantLock()) {
    private val notes = HashMap<String, Note>()

    fun syncFrom(remote: List<Note>) = lock.guarded("NoteCache#sync") {
        for (n in remote) {
            if (n.deleted) return          // "nothing more to do"
            notes[n.id] = n
        }
    }

    fun get(id: String): Note? = lock.guarded("NoteCache#get") { notes[id] }
}

syncFrom runs on a background thread; get runs on main during list binding.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug(s), explain the mechanism, and fix the helper so all 14 call sites become safe.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Do not touch the cache on the main thread" or "replace ReentrantLock with synchronized". Moving get off main hides the ANR but leaves the lock held forever, so the next background call deadlocks instead. Switching to synchronized happens to fix it (stdlib synchronized uses finally), but they cannot say why.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Do the ANRs correlate with sync payloads containing deleted notes? That points straight at the early return.
    • Are there other exits from block: exceptions from notes[...], ConcurrentModificationException, or CancellationException if a call site is inside a coroutine?
    • Who else holds this lock? If anything is reentrant, a ReentrantLock held by a dead code path on a pool thread stays held by that thread.
    • Are the unbalanced Perfetto sections on the same thread as the lock holder?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the helper (one function, all 14 sites benefit), and as a stopgap remote-disable the sync path for deleted notes if the feature flag exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The return inside the lambda is a non-local return: guarded is inline, so it exits syncFrom directly, skipping unlock() and endSection(). The background thread keeps the lock; main later blocks in lock().
    • (b) An exception thrown from block skips unlock() the same way. No finally.
    • (c) Room upgrade introduced a slow query. Traces show main parked on ReentrantLock, not in SQLite, so no.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • (a): JVM unit test: call syncFrom(listOf(deletedNote)), then assert lock.isLocked == false. It fails. Decompile to see the return jump past unlock().
    • (b): unit test where block throws; same assertion.
    • (c): Perfetto main-thread slice shows the lock() park with no SQLite frames; Room's executor threads are idle.
  5. Root cause: The inline helper does cleanup as straight-line code after block(). Because the lambda is inlined, a bare return in it becomes a real return from syncFrom, and control never reaches unlock() or Trace.endSection(). Exceptions do the same. The lock stays owned by the background thread forever, so the next get() on main parks until the ANR watchdog fires. Kotlin is behaving as designed: non-local returns from inline lambdas are allowed, and they run finally blocks, but there was no finally.
  6. Fix: Short-term, fix the helper once: 
    import android.os.Trace
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock

inline fun <T> ReentrantLock.guarded(section: String, block: () -> T): T {
    Trace.beginSection(section)
    try {
        lock()
        try {
            return block()
        } finally {
            unlock()
        }
    } finally {
        Trace.endSection()
    }
}
    Even simpler: use what already exists. stdlib kotlin.concurrent.withLock is inline and unlocks in finally, and androidx.tracing.trace(label) { } is inline and ends the section in finally: 
    import androidx.tracing.trace
import kotlin.concurrent.withLock

fun syncFrom(remote: List<Note>) = trace("NoteCache#sync") {
    lock.withLock {
        for (n in remote) {
            if (n.deleted) continue      // also fix the intent: skip, do not exit
            notes[n.id] = n
        }
    }
}
    Also note the second logic bug: the author wanted "skip deleted notes", so return should have been continue anyway. Long-term: NoteCache.get should not take a lock on main at all. Publish an immutable snapshot through a StateFlow or @Volatile reference, so readers never block (chunk 21 covers the synchronization options).
  7. Prevention:
    • Rule: any inline function that acquires a resource must release it in finally. Better, ban hand-rolled lock or trace helpers and use withLock / trace.
    • Unit tests for helpers that check release on normal return, non-local return and exception.
    • StrictMode and a main-thread lock-wait metric in debug builds; Perfetto in CI for startup and list scroll.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the helper non-inline just to forbid non-local returns. That fixes return but not exceptions, and breaks call sites that use non-local returns legitimately. I would not move all reads off main as the fix; it hides the leaked lock.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• If a call site is in a coroutine and block calls a suspend function, is ReentrantLock safe? → No. After suspension the coroutine may resume on another thread, and unlock() from a different thread throws IllegalMonitorStateException. Use Mutex for suspend code (chunk 14/21).
  • Does a non-local return run finally in an inline function? → Yes. The return goes through the finally because it is all one method after inlining.
  • Would Trace.endSection() on the wrong thread be a problem? → Yes. beginSection/endSection pair per thread; ending on another thread corrupts both threads' slices.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team wrote their own inline fun timed {} to log durations; a return in one call site skipped the "end" log, and the dashboards showed a 0 percent completion rate for a flow that worked fine. Replacing it with a try/finally version fixed the data, and a review rule now asks "what happens on early return?" for every inline helper.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: moves work off main or adds timeouts; does not connect return in an inline lambda with skipped cleanup.
  • Hire: identifies the non-local return and missing finally, fixes the helper with try/finally or withLock.
  • Strong hire: also covers exceptions, the per-thread trace pairing, the continue intent bug, ReentrantLock with suspend, and removes the main-thread lock entirely.
