A fintech app (900k DAU) upgrades Kotlin 1.9.24 to 2.0.x and, in the same PR, AGP to a newer version (red herring: R8 behavior changes are in the release notes too). Staged rollout at 5 percent. Crash-free users drop from 99.85 to 99.2 percent. Top crash:

java.lang.ClassCastException: com.app.transfer.TransferFragment$$ExternalSyntheticLambda3
    cannot be cast to java.io.Serializable
  at com.app.ui.ConfirmDialog$Companion.newInstance(ConfirmDialog.kt:22)
  at com.app.transfer.TransferFragment.onSendClicked(TransferFragment.kt:118)

Second, quieter signal: the "duplicate tap" analytics de-duplicator, keyed by handler.toString(), now reports zero duplicates. The code:

class ConfirmDialog : DialogFragment() {
    companion object {
        fun newInstance(message: String, onConfirm: () -> Unit) = ConfirmDialog().apply {
            arguments = bundleOf("msg" to message, "cb" to (onConfirm as Serializable))
        }
    }
    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog {
        @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST", "DEPRECATION")
        val cb = requireArguments().getSerializable("cb") as () -> Unit
        return AlertDialog.Builder(requireContext())
            .setMessage(requireArguments().getString("msg"))
            .setPositiveButton("OK") { _, _ -> cb() }
            .create()
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What changed, how do you stop the bleeding, and what is the right fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "R8 stripped the Serializable interface; add a keep rule" or "Kotlin 2.0 is buggy, roll back". They do not know the lambda compilation default changed, and they miss that this pattern was broken before the upgrade too.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does the crash reproduce in a debug build without R8? If yes, R8 is not the cause.
    • How many places cast lambdas to Serializable or use lambda toString()/class names as keys? A grep for as Serializable and .toString() on function-typed values gives the blast radius.
    • Did the old code ever crash on process death or "Don't keep activities"? That tells me whether the pattern was already broken.
    • Can we halt the rollout and ship a hotfix in the same train?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout at 5 percent. Fastest safe hotfix if needed: annotate the affected lambdas with @JvmSerializableLambda or set -Xlambdas=class in that module, which restores the 1.x class-based lambdas. That is a stopgap, not the fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Kotlin 2.0 compiles lambdas with invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory by default. On Android, D8 desugars them into $$ExternalSyntheticLambda classes that do not implement Serializable. The old Kotlin lambda classes extended kotlin.jvm.internal.Lambda, which is Serializable, so the cast used to succeed.
    • (b) R8 removed an interface. R8 does not strip Serializable from classes that declare it, and the class name in the stack is a D8 synthetic, which points to (a).
    • (c) AGP desugaring change. Lambda desugaring itself is old and stable; what changed is the input.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • (a): debug build, no minification: println(onConfirm is Serializable) prints false on 2.0 and true on 1.9. "Show Kotlin Bytecode" shows invokedynamic at the call site. The 2.0 "What's new" page documents this change and the three limitations (not serializable, no reflect(), different toString()).
    • (b): same crash with isMinifyEnabled = false rules it out.
    • (c): building the same code with Kotlin 1.9 and the new AGP does not crash.
  5. Root cause: The default lambda compilation strategy changed in Kotlin 2.0. The code relied on an implementation detail (lambdas being Serializable as a side effect of the old class scheme) and on toString() being stable and unique. Neither was a contract. The deeper issue is that the pattern was already wrong: the lambda captured TransferFragment (to call viewModel.send()), so on process death or config change, serializing it either threw NotSerializableException (Fragment is not serializable) or restored a lambda pointing at a dead Fragment. That was showing up as a low-volume RuntimeException: Parcelable encountered IOException writing serializable object that nobody had prioritized.
  6. Fix: Short-term: @JvmSerializableLambda on the few affected lambdas to unblock the release, with a ticket and a deadline. Long-term: callbacks never go into Bundles. Use the Fragment Result API so the result survives config change and process death without capturing anything: 
    class ConfirmDialog : DialogFragment() {
    companion object {
        const val REQUEST_KEY = "confirm_transfer"
        fun newInstance(message: String) = ConfirmDialog().apply {
            arguments = bundleOf("msg" to message)
        }
    }
    override fun onCreateDialog(savedInstanceState: Bundle?): Dialog =
        AlertDialog.Builder(requireContext())
            .setMessage(requireArguments().getString("msg"))
            .setPositiveButton("OK") { _, _ ->
                setFragmentResult(REQUEST_KEY, bundleOf("confirmed" to true))
            }
            .create()
}

// In TransferFragment.onViewCreated (or onCreate):
// childFragmentManager.setFragmentResultListener(ConfirmDialog.REQUEST_KEY, viewLifecycleOwner) { _, b ->
//     if (b.getBoolean("confirmed")) viewModel.send()
// }
    (Use childFragmentManager if the dialog is shown from it, parentFragmentManager otherwise; they must match.) For the analytics de-duplicator, key on a stable explicit ID (action name plus target ID), never on a lambda's identity or string form.
  7. Prevention:
    • Lint/Detekt rule or a simple CI grep that flags as Serializable on function types and toString() on function-typed values.
    • Test config-change and process-death paths ("Don't keep activities", ActivityScenario.recreate()) for every dialog.
    • For compiler upgrades, read the compatibility guide's "behavioral" entries and do a dedicated rollout, not bundled with AGP.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set -Xlambdas=class project-wide permanently. It gives up the binary-size win and keeps a broken pattern alive. I would not roll back Kotlin 2.0 entirely if a targeted hotfix exists; K2 brings other value and rolling back costs a whole train.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did toString() keys report zero duplicates? → Each D8 synthetic lambda's toString() is the default ClassName@identityHash. Capturing lambdas are new objects per tap, so every key is unique. Before, with kotlin-reflect, Kotlin lambdas printed a type signature that was identical for both taps.
  • Would bundleOf("cb" to onConfirm) without the explicit cast have helped? → It would fail differently: bundleOf throws IllegalArgumentException for an unsupported value type at runtime.
  • Is there any legitimate need for serializable lambdas? → Rare on Android. Some JVM frameworks (Spark, some Java serialization-based caches) need them; that is what @JvmSerializableLambda exists for.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A compiler upgrade went out with an "it compiles, ship it" review. The crash came from a lambda cast that a reviewer had flagged two years earlier as "works, but fragile". The fix took a day; the lesson was to treat compiler "behavioral change" entries like a dependency's breaking-change notes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames R8 or proposes a keep rule; does not know the 2.0 lambda change.
  • Hire: identifies indy lambdas as non-serializable, knows @JvmSerializableLambda / -Xlambdas=class, halts the rollout.
  • Strong hire: explains D8 desugaring, explains the toString() de-dup failure, shows the pattern was already broken by process death and Fragment capture, and moves to the Fragment Result API with prevention in CI.

questions.subtopic: Higher-order function cost in hot paths
questions.contextHtml:
A trading app (600k DAU, 40 percent devices are low-end with 3 GB RAM and 90 Hz or 120 Hz screens on mid-range) renders a live price chart as a custom View. Product wants 5,000 points per series, 2 series, smooth at the display's refresh rate. On a mid-range test device, p95 frame time is 21 ms at 120 Hz (budget 8.3 ms) and logcat shows frequent Background concurrent copying GC freed ... lines while the chart animates. A teammate suspects Path complexity and hardware acceleration (red herring: the Path is rebuilt only when data changes, every 500 ms). Code:

class PriceChartView(context: Context) : View(context) {
    var series: List<FloatArray> = emptyList()
    private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG)

    private fun drawSeries(
        canvas: Canvas,
        ys: FloatArray,
        mapX: (Int) -> Float,
        mapY: (Float) -> Float,
    ) {
        for (i in 1 until ys.size) {
            canvas.drawLine(mapX(i - 1), mapY(ys[i - 1]), mapX(i), mapY(ys[i]), paint)
        }
    }

    override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) {
        val w = width.toFloat(); val h = height.toFloat()
        series.forEach { ys ->
            val min = ys.min(); val max = ys.max()
            drawSeries(
                canvas, ys,
                mapX = { i -> i * w / (ys.size - 1) },
                mapY = { v -> h - (v - min) / (max - min) * h },
            )
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Where do the allocations come from, quantify them, and how would you fix it? Would you just make drawSeries inline?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn off anti-aliasing" or "use a SurfaceView". Or "make everything inline" without knowing why, which does fix this case but is applied by habit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is onDraw called every frame during the animation? (An invalidate loop for a crosshair or price ticker would explain per-frame cost.)
    • What does the allocation tracker show per frame? I want evidence before changing code.
    • Do we need individual line segments, or would one drawLines(FloatArray) call be acceptable visually?
    • Device mix: is 21 ms on the mid-range device or the low-end one?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, but if the feature is behind a flag, ship with 1,000 points on low-end devices while the fix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Boxing through function types. (Int) -> Float and (Float) -> Float are Function1<Integer, Float> / Function1<Float, Float>. Every invoke boxes its argument and result. Float.valueOf has no cache, so every Float box allocates; Integer.valueOf caches only -128..127.
    • (b) Capturing lambda objects created per series per frame (they capture w, h, ys, min, max). Small: 4 objects per frame.
    • (c) drawLine call overhead: 10,000 JNI-ish canvas calls per frame. Real but secondary.
    • (d) Path/hardware acceleration. Path is not used per frame; ruled out.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Android Studio Memory Profiler, "Record Java/Kotlin allocations" during animation: I expect java.lang.Float and java.lang.Integer dominating, allocated from drawSeries.
    • Math check: per segment there are 4 calls, each boxing input and output: about 8 allocations. 5,000 points times 2 series is about 10,000 segments, so about 80,000 allocations per frame (a bit fewer for cached small Integers). At 120 frames per second that is about 9.6M allocations per second, around 150 MB/s at 16 bytes per box. That explains the GC log.
    • Perfetto system trace: GC slices overlapping Choreographer#doFrame on the render thread's input side, and onDraw duration per frame.
  5. Root cause: A non-inline higher-order function with primitive-typed function parameters called in a hot inner loop. The lambda bodies are tiny, but the call goes through the generic Function1.invoke(Object): Object bridge, so every argument and result is boxed. The GC churn and the interface calls push frame time over budget.
  6. Fix: Option A, smallest change: make drawSeries inline. The lambdas passed as literals are pasted into the loop, so mapX/mapY become plain float arithmetic with no Function1, no boxing, no lambda objects. It is private, small, and has two call sites, so code size and ABI do not matter. This is the textbook case where inline pays. Option B, better overall: precompute and draw in one batch. 
    import android.graphics.Canvas
import android.graphics.Paint
import android.view.View
import android.content.Context

class PriceChartView(context: Context) : View(context) {
    var series: List<FloatArray> = emptyList()
        set(value) { field = value; buffers = value.map { FloatArray((it.size - 1) * 4) }; invalidate() }
    private var buffers: List<FloatArray> = emptyList()
    private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG)

    override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) {
        val w = width.toFloat(); val h = height.toFloat()
        for (s in series.indices) {
            val ys = series[s]; val pts = buffers[s]
            if (ys.size < 2) continue
            val min = ys.min(); val range = (ys.max() - min).takeIf { it > 0f } ?: 1f
            val dx = w / (ys.size - 1)
            var j = 0
            for (i in 1 until ys.size) {           // plain primitives, no lambdas
                pts[j++] = (i - 1) * dx; pts[j++] = h - (ys[i - 1] - min) / range * h
                pts[j++] = i * dx;       pts[j++] = h - (ys[i] - min) / range * h
            }
            canvas.drawLines(pts, paint)           // one call per series
        }
    }
}
    That removes boxing, removes per-frame lambda objects, reuses buffers, and replaces 10,000 draw calls with 2. It also fixes a latent division by zero when all prices are equal (max == min). If the mapping must stay pluggable (a library API), use a fun interface ValueMapper { fun map(v: Float): Float }. Its method has a primitive signature, so no boxing, and it can be stored, unlike an inlined lambda.
  7. Prevention:
    • A macrobenchmark (FrameTimingMetric) for the chart screen in CI with a frame-time budget per device class.
    • Review rule for onDraw, onMeasure, onBindViewHolder and Compose draw lambdas: no non-inline function-type calls with primitive parameters in inner loops, no allocations per frame.
    • Allocation tracking in the perf checklist before merging custom views.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make inline a blanket rule for all helpers; here it works because the function is private, small, and hot. I would not switch to SurfaceView or OpenGL before removing 9.6M allocations per second; that is a big rewrite for a problem that is plain boxing. I would not micro-optimize the forEach over series: it is inline and runs twice per frame.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• If drawSeries were inline but callers passed stored val mapper: (Float) -> Float, would boxing go away? → No. The function object already exists, and inlining just calls mapper.invoke(...) through the boxed bridge. Inline helps only for lambda literals or references at the call site.
  • What about Compose Canvas { }? → Same rule: the DrawScope lambda runs per frame, so avoid boxing function-type calls and allocations inside it; cache with remember and read state in the draw phase.
  • Would the JIT remove the boxing via escape analysis? → Do not count on it. ART's optimizing compiler does some, but it is not reliable for this pattern; the allocation profile is the source of truth.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A heatmap view mapped values through a (Float) -> Int color function per cell, 40,000 cells per frame. Jank on mid-range devices looked like a GPU issue for a week. One allocation recording showed millions of java.lang.Float objects; a primitive fun interface cut frame time by more than half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: guesses at GPU or anti-aliasing; cannot explain why lambdas allocate here.
  • Hire: identifies boxing through Function1, proposes inline or a primitive fun interface, verifies with the allocation profiler.
  • Strong hire: quantifies allocations per frame and per second, knows Float has no box cache, batches with drawLines and reuses buffers, knows when inline does not help (stored function values), and adds a frame-timing benchmark.

You own an internal analytics SDK (core-analytics) consumed by the main app and by a partner's prebuilt AAR (partner-payments, compiled by another team on their own schedule, last built against SDK 3.1). SDK 3.1 had:

public inline fun track(event: String, props: () -> Map<String, Any?> = { emptyMap() }) {
    if (Analytics.isEnabled) internalSend(event, props())
}
@PublishedApi internal fun internalSend(event: String, props: Map<String, Any?>) { /* ... */ }

A privacy bug: track sent props even when the user had opted out of "personalized analytics", because it only checked isEnabled. SDK 3.2 fixed track to also check Analytics.consentGranted. The main app upgraded to 3.2. Two weeks later a privacy audit found the partner payments screens still sending personalized props for opted-out users (about 70k users). Then SDK 3.3 renamed internalSend to dispatch "since it's internal anyway", and the app started crashing on the payments screen:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: No static method internalSend(Ljava/lang/String;Ljava/util/Map;)V
    in class Lcom/app/analytics/TrackKt; or its super classes
  at com.partner.payments.CheckoutFragment.onPay(CheckoutFragment.kt:88)

Red herring: 3.3 also enabled R8 full mode in the sample app.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened mechanically, why did both problems slip through, and what would you change in the SDK's API and process?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "R8 removed internalSend; add a keep rule" and "the partner should upgrade". It misses that the privacy fix never reached precompiled code, and that @PublishedApi made an "internal" function part of the binary ABI.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which artifacts contain inlined copies of track? Any module compiled outside the app build (prebuilt AARs, partner SDKs) is suspect.
    • Does the payments AAR's bytecode call TrackKt.internalSend directly? javap -c or decompiling the AAR answers it in minutes.
    • Is the server able to drop personalized props for opted-out users? That is the fastest data-side mitigation.
    • What other public inline functions does the SDK expose?
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Crash: ship 3.3.1 restoring internalSend with the old signature as a @PublishedApi internal (or @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN) public) function that delegates to the new path. Do not wait for the partner.
    • Privacy: server-side filter that drops personalized props when the consent flag for that user is off; purge collected data per the privacy team's process; ask the partner to rebuild against 3.3.1.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Public inline function bodies are copied into the consumer at the consumer's compile time. The partner AAR contains the 3.1 body (checks only isEnabled), so the 3.2 fix never ran there.
    • (b) The partner's inlined 3.1 body calls internalSend by name. @PublishedApi made it binary-public. Renaming it in 3.3 removed a symbol precompiled code links against, giving NoSuchMethodError.
    • (c) R8 full mode stripped the method. Possible in principle, but the method no longer exists in the SDK's own classes at all, and the sample app's R8 setting does not affect the main app.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • (a)/(b): decompile CheckoutFragment from the AAR. Expect Analytics.isEnabled() check inline and an invokestatic TrackKt.internalSend, with no consent check.
    • (c): build the app with minification off; the crash still happens. apkanalyzer dex packages shows dispatch present and internalSend absent.
    • Run binary-compatibility-validator's apiCheck against the 3.1 .api dump: it flags internalSend as removed.
  5. Root cause: Two consequences of one design choice: a public inline function with real logic. (1) Behavior lives in consumers' bytecode, so a fix in the SDK does not apply to anything compiled earlier. (2) Everything that body calls must be binary-public, and @PublishedApi internal hides that in source while freezing it in ABI. The process gap: no ABI check in CI, and a mental model of "internal means we can rename it".
  6. Fix: Short-term: 3.3.1 with the old symbol restored as a delegating shim. Long-term, make the inline surface a thin, stable trampoline and move all policy into a non-inline function: 
    // Inline only to avoid allocating the props lambda when disabled; no policy here.
public inline fun track(event: String, props: () -> Map<String, Any?> = { emptyMap() }) {
    if (Analytics.shouldCollect(event)) Analytics.send(event, props())
}

public object Analytics {
    @Volatile @PublishedApi internal var enabled: Boolean = false
    // Non-inline: policy (enabled, consent, sampling) can change in any release.
    public fun shouldCollect(event: String): Boolean = enabled && consentGranted()
    public fun send(event: String, props: Map<String, Any?>) { /* scrub + enqueue */ }
    private fun consentGranted(): Boolean = true
}
    Privacy-critical checks also run again inside send (defense in depth), so even a stale inlined caller cannot bypass them. Keep old @PublishedApi symbols for at least one major version, marked @Deprecated(level = DeprecationLevel.HIDDEN) so new code cannot see them but old binaries still link.
  7. Prevention:
    • binary-compatibility-validator in CI; .api file changes need SDK-owner review. It includes @PublishedApi declarations.
    • Policy: no business or privacy logic in public inline bodies. Inline only for allocation-avoiding trampolines and reified wrappers.
    • Consumer matrix test: run the previous version of partner AARs against the new SDK in CI to catch NoSuchMethodError before release.
    • Document in the SDK changelog which functions are inline, and that fixes there require consumers to recompile.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove inline entirely: the lazy props lambda avoids building maps on hot paths when analytics is off, which is a real win across thousands of call sites. I would not add R8 keep rules; the method is gone from source, so there is nothing to keep. I would not rely on the partner to "just rebuild" as the privacy fix; server and non-inline checks must protect users regardless of consumer build dates.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would making track non-inline have prevented the privacy bug? → Yes for future fixes, since the body would run from the SDK. The partner would still need to rebuild once to stop calling the old inlined code.
  • Can @PublishedApi be applied to private declarations? → No. It applies to internal declarations (and has effect on them only); private members cannot be called from public inline functions.
  • Does this affect a single-repo app with many Gradle modules? → Much less, since all modules recompile together. It matters for anything prebuilt: AARs from other teams, published libraries, binaries cached across builds with different versions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A logging library fixed PII redaction inside a public inline log {}. Months later a security scan found unredacted logs from a module vendored as a JAR. The library added a non-inline redaction pass inside its sink and published a rule that inline bodies may only decide whether to evaluate the lambda.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames R8; thinks upgrading the dependency updates already-compiled callers.
  • Hire: explains that inline bodies are copied at compile time and that @PublishedApi functions are binary-public; restores the symbol.
  • Strong hire: separates the privacy and crash timelines, adds server-side and non-inline defense in depth, reshapes the API to a thin trampoline, adds binary-compatibility-validator and a consumer-matrix test, and keeps old symbols hidden but present.

questions.contextHtml:
Your team has 60 ViewModels with copy-pasted loading/error logic. The tech lead asks for one shared helper, with these requirements gathered in a meeting (partly contradictory):

  • "Works from suspend code (repository calls) and from plain code (validation)."
  • "Callers should be able to bail out early, like return when input is invalid."
  • "Must show a loading spinner during the work and always hide it, even on errors."
  • "Should not swallow coroutine cancellation."
  • "Keep APK size impact small" (the app is at 48 MB, budget 50 MB).

Three proposals are on the table:

// A: inline, generic block
inline fun <T> withLoading(state: MutableStateFlow<Boolean>, block: () -> T): T { ... }

// B: suspend, non-inline
suspend fun <T> withLoading(state: MutableStateFlow<Boolean>, block: suspend () -> T): T { ... }

// C: launches for the caller
fun ViewModel.launchWithLoading(state: MutableStateFlow<Boolean>, block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit): Job
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and why? Show the implementation and explain how each requirement is met or consciously dropped.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Option C, because it is the least code at call sites" without discussing early return or cancellation, or "Option A because inline is faster" without noting it must use try/finally and how it interacts with suspend.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does "bail out early" mean leaving the calling function (return from the ViewModel method) or just stopping the helper's block? It decides whether non-local return is required.
    • Is loading state per screen (one flag) or per operation? With concurrent operations, a single Boolean flips off when the first finishes; a counter or per-operation state is needed.
    • Who owns error handling: the helper (maps to UiState.Error) or the caller? I would keep the helper to loading only.
    • How many call sites? 60 ViewModels, maybe 200 calls. That decides whether inline code size matters.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. I would prototype on two ViewModels and measure APK delta before rolling out.
  3. Options, ranked:
    • (A) Inline with a plain () -> T block. Inline lambdas are transparent to suspension: if the caller is a suspend function, the block can call suspend functions, because the body is pasted into the caller. It also allows non-local return from the calling function. With try/finally, the spinner always turns off, including on non-local return, exception and cancellation. Code size: the wrapper is about a dozen bytecode instructions, times about 200 sites, so a few KB at most. Meets every requirement.
    • (B) Suspend, non-inline. Clear and debuggable, but cannot be called from non-suspend code, the block cannot do non-local return, and every call allocates a suspend lambda object (a class with a state machine). Fails two requirements.
    • (C) Launches for the caller. Convenient, but it hides launch (callers cannot await results or compose it into a larger suspend function), non-local return is impossible because the block runs later in another coroutine, and if someone makes it inline the block would need crossinline anyway. Good as a thin convenience on top of A, not as the primitive.
  4. How I'd verify the choice:
    • Unit tests with runTest: spinner state after normal return, non-local return, exception, and cancellation (cancel the job mid-delay and assert the flag is false).
    • APK Analyzer diff on the prototype branch for size.
    • A quick check that call sites in both suspend and non-suspend functions compile.
  5. Key mechanism (why A works): Inlining copies both the helper body and the lambda into the caller. So the lambda runs in the caller's frame: suspend calls are legal when the caller is suspend, return exits the caller, and a finally in the helper is part of the same method, so it runs on every exit path. Cancellation arrives as a CancellationException from a suspension point inside the block; since the helper does not catch anything, it propagates, and finally resets the flag.
  6. Implementation: 
    import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update

// Counter, not Boolean: two overlapping operations must not hide each other's spinner.
inline fun <T> MutableStateFlow<Int>.withLoading(block: () -> T): T {
    update { it + 1 }
    try {
        return block()
    } finally {
        update { it - 1 }            // runs on return, non-local return, throw, cancellation
    }
}

class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: ProfileRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val loadingCount = MutableStateFlow(0)
    val isLoading = loadingCount.map { it > 0 }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), false)

    fun save(name: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            loadingCount.withLoading {
                if (name.isBlank()) return@launch     // early exit; finally still runs
                repo.save(name)                       // suspend call inside inline lambda
            }
        }
    }

    fun validate(input: String): Boolean = loadingCount.withLoading { input.length in 3..40 }
}
    No catch in the helper, so cancellation and errors propagate to the caller, which decides how to show them (chunk 19 covers error strategies). If the team wants C's convenience, it is a three-line non-inline wrapper: fun ViewModel.launchWithLoading(c: MutableStateFlow<Int>, block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit) = viewModelScope.launch { c.withLoading { block() } }.
  7. Prevention / guardrails:
    • Tests above live next to the helper; they are the contract.
    • KDoc states: "non-local return and suspend calls allowed; never catches; loading count always restored".
    • Lint or review note: do not wrap the block in runCatching inside the helper (it would swallow CancellationException).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch Exception in the helper to "be safe"; that swallows cancellation and hides bugs. I would not use a Boolean flag if operations can overlap. I would not expose it as a public library API across separately compiled modules without thinking about Q086's ABI rules; inside one app build it is fine. I consciously drop "helper handles errors" from the requirements, because combining loading and error policy in one inline function makes every call site's bytecode carry error mapping too.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a caller launches a coroutine inside the block, withLoading { scope.launch { repo.save() } }? → The block returns immediately after launch, so the spinner turns off before the work finishes. The helper only covers work done in the block itself; document that, or use option C for fire-and-forget.
  • Why not inline with crossinline block? → crossinline is only needed if the helper calls the block inside another lambda or object. A does not, and adding it would remove the non-local return the team asked for.
  • Can the inline block call suspend functions if the caller is not suspend? → No. Suspend calls require a suspend context; in validate() the block is non-suspend code, and the compiler enforces that per call site.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team standardized on a non-inline suspend fun withLoading(block: suspend () -> T). Within a month, developers had copy-pasted a second version for non-suspend code and a third that caught Exception "to hide the spinner on failure", which broke cancellation on back-press. Replacing all three with one inline try/finally helper and four tests removed about 300 lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by call-site brevity; no finally; catches Exception.
  • Hire: picks the inline option, explains suspend transparency and non-local return, uses try/finally.
  • Strong hire: also handles overlapping operations with a counter, keeps cancellation propagating, quantifies code size, explains why crossinline would be wrong here, layers the launch convenience on top, and lists which requirement was dropped and why.
